title: Urban expansion and the collapse of tropical stream ecosystems
methods: comparative field sampling along an urban-cover gradient
body-size spectrum fitting (maximum likelihood, Edwards et al. 2017)

core_conclusion: Along an urban-cover gradient in the Metropolitan Region of São Paulo, stream biodiversity loss is strongly non-random with respect to body mass: very small, moderately large and large taxa are selectively lost, truncating community size spectra and compressing size ranges by four orders of magnitude relative to rainforest streams. Food-web complexity collapses from more than 150 trophic links to as few as 3, producing a 1,446-fold reduction in energy flow - a loss of ecosystem function, not merely of species richness.
why_it_matters: Shows that species counts badly understate the functional damage urbanization does to streams, because energy flux falls by orders of magnitude more than diversity; identifies body mass as the mechanistic link from land cover to ecosystem service; defines a functional restoration target (size-spectrum slope, link density, flux) using rainforest headwaters in the same basin as the reference state; and does so in a Global South megacity where most future urban growth will occur and where stream self-purification underpins failing sanitation infrastructure.
why_nature: A generalizable mechanism drawn from a single megacity; a causal chain running from catchment urban cover through community size structure and food-web topology to energy and carbon flow; headline effect sizes that are derived from metabolic scaling rather than reported as raw contrasts; under-represented Global South urban evidence; and policy-translatable functional endpoints for sanitation, riparian-buffer and stream-daylighting decisions.
added_value_to_my_research: Explainable ML on MapBiomas covariates -> wall-to-wall stream-condition surface with threshold attribution for the MRSP
Physics-informed graph operator with metabolic-scaling and mass-balance priors -> transferable to urban flow networks
Flux loss as a mediating exposure -> 2SFCA-style sanitation and stream-exposure accessibility index for health geography
MapBiomas 1985-present trajectories + spatiotemporal KDE -> time-since-urbanization, lag and hysteresis in urban outcomes
Agent-based restoration-siting optimizer with an equity constraint -> ecological analogue of my EV-charging efficiency-vs-equity work
